body:
When an approval reaches the effect
A report has been reviewed and approved. Before release, the document service that prepared it changes a passage to answer an objection. Does the earlier approval still apply? A record saying only “approved” leaves the next participant to invent the answer.
The useful decision identifies the document, the permitted use and the version the person examined. The release path can then compare what it is about to do with what was accepted. This is where an independent judgment meets the machinery that carries its consequence. Across a network of reused AI capabilities, the kind DAOnet’s design describes, that connection would let a contributor and a receiving team coordinate an actual use, rather than rely on a catalogue entry’s general promise.
The version travels with the decision
The relationship is small enough to state explicitly:
Step in the hypothetical release	Object that must remain identifiable	
Propose the document	The particular document version and intended use	
Review and decide	The reviewer, decision scope and version examined	
Attempt the release	The actual version presented to the release path	
Record the result	What was permitted or refused, and whether the release occurred	
Approval of version one does not answer the request to release version two. The release path needs to compare them and return the changed work for a relevant decision. An independent record makes an invented approval harder to conceal; a constrained release path makes bypassing the decision harder. A faithful record cannot stop an unrestricted upload credential, while a gate checking an untrustworthy assertion can enforce the wrong decision efficiently.
A decision to permit the release is also different from the release happening. The tool may fail, the destination may be unavailable or the attempt may stop before the document becomes accessible. Recording only the permission would leave the participants without an account of the consequence they were trying to govern.
An article makes the same distinction familiar. Its author corrects a paragraph after review; the publisher now has different words to examine. Gazette can build the corrected page, but a successful build cannot accept the new paragraph on the publisher’s behalf. The writing, its rendered page and the decision to release it each need to remain identifiable.
YojnAI’s proposed improvement workflow put a similar distinction inside the application: feedback on a trace, a candidate improvement job, inspection of its result and an explicit push of a chosen version were separate steps. A one-click return to an earlier version belonged to that deployment design. By contrast, a partner application’s trace service could update feedback on an event row; changing that assessment was not itself a decision to deploy different application behaviour. Choosing a version needs the link from reviewed evidence to the actual effect.
Another route can undo the arrangement
Suppose the release tool faithfully rejects the changed document, but the service also holds an unrestricted credential to upload it directly. The court that judges an action before it happens has examined the request without governing the consequence. The second route has to be brought into the arrangement or removed before the judgment can do its intended work.
Another actor able to replace the document afterwards creates a related dependency. Following those routes tells us where the control actually reaches and where somebody else's responsibility begins. A common record can make a departure visible; the path carrying the action gives the decision its practical force.
The same question applies to an urgent correction. A process can provide a narrow route for it without making every release depend on a general policy amendment. That route still needs an identifiable decision, a scope and an account of the resulting version. Otherwise the exception becomes an alternative publication path with fewer constraints, rather than a way to handle the specific need.
What the shared account contributes
The statements entering the common record still depend on their sources. If one participant asserts that a document was approved, the record needs a way to identify the approving party and the decision's scope. If a physical event happened outside the system, a ledger entry cannot manufacture observation of it. Agreement about a recorded statement and evidence for the event are connected but different parts of the arrangement.
This helps make the architectural choice more precise. Which disagreement does the shared mechanism resolve? Is the concern an operator altering records, participants seeing incompatible versions or a single organisation controlling access? Signed records or a shared database may answer the particular problem more simply. A new chain also requires adoption, infrastructure and a way to handle its own failures.
The document service makes the ambition concrete. A particular version meets a decision, that decision governs a release and the resulting record lets participants examine whether the consequence matched what was accepted. A shared mechanism earns its place if it makes this relationship more dependable across the people involved. The useful achievement is a consequence connected to accountable judgment, with a record people can use to understand and contest it.

body:
Some things never change. It’s time they do…
Okay. Before we get into AI interoperability and the possible role of a blockchain, a refresher.
What is a blockchain? In its most rudimentary form, a ledger. A better one, or a worse one, depending on the use case. Cryptography helps participants verify records; a consensus mechanism determines which history they accept. The familiar operations of creating, reading, updating and deleting data take a different shape when participants need to agree on a shared record. “Immutable” is shorthand for resistance to rewriting under the system's security assumptions, not a magical exemption from attack. Once you have that ledger, you can do cool shit with it. DeFi was all the craze a couple of years before I wrote this in May 2024.
And a neural network? At this level of abstraction, a function approximator. Think of a sine wave and the periodic functions it suggests; then think of aperiodic, linear and nonlinear relationships. Given data spread through an n-dimensional space, can a network learn a useful relationship among the values? Fitting those examples is one part. Generalising beyond them is what makes the result useful. I hear “generation” is all the craze these days.
Cool. That's it. No more extra-credit assignments from this point on.
I lied. There's one more thing.
What's an API? A defined way for software systems to talk to each other. A really awesome one, sometimes. Its usefulness depends on what it lets the other system do.
The interface stayed familiar
Software had decades in which to develop its routines, interfaces, deployment practices and containers. Then the post-2022 AI rush made a familiar neighbourhood model, GPT, everyone's business. The question I was asking in 2024 was what happened when we took established software interfaces and translated them almost verbatim into this much younger wave of applications.
Did you read the paragraph above?
Yes or no?
That gives us a simple state to reason about. In an ordinary program, we can often name routines, describe their inputs and outputs, and expose the parts another program needs to call. For a fixed set of inputs and state, a deterministic routine produces a fixed result. Randomness and concurrency can complicate that behaviour, while the named routines still give us parts to examine and compose.
A trained neural network offers a different problem. We can see its architecture and, where available, its parameters. That does not automatically give us a set of independent, named abilities that can be lifted out and used like ordinary routines. Knowing where multiplication occurs is not the same as knowing where “understands a supplier's exception” lives.
Yet the familiar request-and-response interface is often the first thing we build around it. That is useful. It can also conceal the part we have not learned how to separate.
Consider Docker and the software engineering practices around containers. They arrived through years of testing, adoption and adjustment. The AI application rush was trying to compress a comparable maturation into a couple of years. Two years versus decades. What could go wrong?
Plenty.
Zero or one: which part can another system call?
A modern AI application can look remarkably like an operating system, loosely speaking. Retrieval is part of its input/output path. Context resembles working memory. Agents resemble threads carrying out activities. These are analogies, not literal descriptions of an LLM's internals, but they help locate the work.
A model is invoked at a particular point in the agent flow. The orchestration framework supplies context, remembers intermediate results, chooses the next call and eventually returns an answer. Much of the application's useful behaviour lives in that arrangement around the model.
Now let a second system call it. Suppose the exposed choices are only:
Zero: call the base language model.
One: call the complete orchestrated application and receive its final answer.
Calling that final endpoint from an ordinary application may be entirely sufficient. But when one agent system needs to work with another, the choice is limiting. It may need the state reached halfway through a task, the evidence already collected, or a callback when a particular agent has finished. Starting again at the base model discards useful work. Calling the final endpoint asks for more work than the receiving system needs.
The problem is not that an API is incapable of carrying state. An application can persist memory and expose finer operations. The problem is that a wrapper which exposes only those two endpoints has not done so. Its caller cannot reach the internal memory merely because the application uses agents. And exposing that memory still says nothing about whether learned abilities inside the underlying model are independently reusable.
What we tried with YojnAI
With YojnAI, our approach was to wrap memory states in a data structure and keep caching those states so the application could expose callbacks at the agent level. A caller could work with an intermediate state instead of choosing only between the base model and the final orchestration endpoint.
This also let us “teach” the invoked LLMs to work with the wrapper's memory operations during the application flow. The wrapper kept the states; the model could use those operations. That is different from a neural network acquiring a memory subsystem we could lift out and transplant into another model.
We built utilities on top of that work and called them Apps. Different story. YojnAI's application design follows those parts through the work a customer needed to do.
But even that approach was not enough for the larger question.
A third possibility: combine the learned parts
What I really wanted was a third scenario: a subnet of one neural network working with a subnet of another. Not merely their final answers passing through an endpoint. The learned capacities themselves becoming composable.
Imagine a model M1 containing capacities I1, I2, I3, …, In, realised through subnets which might overlap. Another model, M2, contains capacities K1, K2, K3, …, Kn, again potentially overlapping.
How would you take K2 from M2, and I2 and I3 from M1, to make M3?
Note
Naming a capacity does not isolate it. The notation makes the question easy to write. It does not establish that those capacities are cleanly located, separable or compatible. Overlap is part of the difficulty. Removing the part we call I2 might also remove something I3 relies on. Two representations that work within their own models may not mean the same thing when connected.
There are two different times at which we might attempt the combination:
When the combination happens	The question it raises	
Before deployment, loosely like compilation	Can selected learned components be aligned and assembled into a new model which preserves the wanted capacities?	
During execution, loosely like runtime linking	Can one running system use a selected learned capacity in another, with the representations, state and dependencies needed for that interaction?	
Pre-deployment composition is a research problem of its own. Work such as Git Re-Basin examines a particular route to aligning and merging model weights. The runtime question reaches beyond what a request-and-response wrapper has solved. Transporting a message cannot, by itself, discover a decomposition of the learned computation or make incompatible representations fit.
That was the force of my complaint about the API model. The familiar interface can carry the eventual interaction. It cannot substitute for understanding what is being composed.
My gut said a blockchain might have a role here. A shared record could help parties coordinate contributions, versions or use. It would still need something meaningful to record. The road from a ledger to a working M3 is long and hard.
The inquiry continues in The intelligence between the parts. It asks what must pass between learned capacities for their combination to retain meaning. There is also nearer work we can do without claiming to have solved that problem: make the capabilities we already know how to share intelligible to their next user.
Several different things can look like intelligence
A model, a prompt, a dataset, a workflow and a hosted service can each contribute to a useful result, but the next team receives something different in each case. A dataset provides examples, a prompt supplies instructions in a context and a workflow connects operations. A model contains learned parameters, while an endpoint offers a response with much of its implementation remaining at the provider. These forms carry different dependencies and different opportunities to change the behaviour: adopting a prompt leaves the consumer to supply the model and its context, whereas invoking a service leaves more of the operation with the provider. A useful catalogue makes that contribution and continuing responsibility intelligible, so a team can discover the form it actually needs.
Application composition is a nearer form of reuse
Consider two hypothetical document capabilities. One extracts supplier details from an invoice; another checks a proposed payment against the extracted terms. They can be combined through defined inputs and outputs. The second does not need the first system's entire internal process, but it does need enough context to know what the result means. Was the supplier identity confirmed or merely inferred? Is a payment date absent, or was extraction unsuccessful? Does the returned value refer to this invoice or another record? Each distinction changes what the checking step can do with the answer.
A catalogue entry for that invented extraction capability could carry a compact account rather than a promise of general document understanding:
Part of the capability description	Example declaration	
Object being supplied	A document-extraction workflow, not a trained subnetwork	
Input	A declared family of invoice documents	
Output	Supplier fields and payment terms, with source locations and unresolved values	
Required context	Document identity, language and the selected workflow version	
Evaluation question	Whether supported examples preserve the fields and evidence needed by the payment check	
Boundary	No authority to approve or execute a payment	
Conditions of use	The workflow's licence and dependencies, without any customer's invoice data	
The next component can now ask a particular question of the output. An absent payment date can remain unresolved rather than masquerade as a zero or an extraction success. Another document layout gives the receiving team a case to test, not a reason to assume the same result. The description supplies a starting point for adoption; the receiving application still has to examine the contribution in its own setting.
Versioning is a relationship with downstream work
If the extraction changes, the checking step may change even when its own code does not. A newer model might recognise more layouts and produce a different format. A revised tool might treat a missing field differently. Moving from a source location to a bare value could leave the payment check without the evidence it used to receive. Versioning connects those changes to the downstream work that depends on them; its value comes from identifying relevant behaviour and requirements.
The application needs to identify which capability it used and retain enough context to investigate a regression. Keeping an earlier configuration available can support recovery, provided its dependencies can still be supplied. The practical promise of reuse is less repeated work. Unannounced changes reverse that promise when every consumer has to rediscover the same failure, reconstruct its cause and repair their application separately.
Adoption gives the description a test

Some things never change. It’s time they do…
Okay. Before we get into AI interoperability and the possible role of a blockchain, a refresher.
What is a blockchain? In its most rudimentary form, a ledger. A better one, or a worse one, depending on the use case. Cryptography helps participants verify records; a consensus mechanism determines which history they accept. The familiar operations of creating, reading, updating and deleting data take a different shape when participants need to agree on a shared record. “Immutable” is shorthand for resistance to rewriting under the system's security assumptions, not a magical exemption from attack. Once you have that ledger, you can do cool shit with it. DeFi was all the craze a couple of years before I wrote this in May 2024.
And a neural network? At this level of abstraction, a function approximator. Think of a sine wave and the periodic functions it suggests; then think of aperiodic, linear and nonlinear relationships. Given data spread through an n-dimensional space, can a network learn a useful relationship among the values? Fitting those examples is one part. Generalising beyond them is what makes the result useful. I hear “generation” is all the craze these days.
Cool. That's it. No more extra-credit assignments from this point on.
I lied. There's one more thing.
What's an API? A defined way for software systems to talk to each other. A really awesome one, sometimes. Its usefulness depends on what it lets the other system do.
The interface stayed familiar
Software had decades in which to develop its routines, interfaces, deployment practices and containers. Then the post-2022 AI rush made a familiar neighbourhood model, GPT, everyone's business. The question I was asking in 2024 was what happened when we took established software interfaces and translated them almost verbatim into this much younger wave of applications.
Did you read the paragraph above?
Yes or no?
That gives us a simple state to reason about. In an ordinary program, we can often name routines, describe their inputs and outputs, and expose the parts another program needs to call. For a fixed set of inputs and state, a deterministic routine produces a fixed result. Randomness and concurrency can complicate that behaviour, while the named routines still give us parts to examine and compose.
A trained neural network offers a different problem. We can see its architecture and, where available, its parameters. That does not automatically give us a set of independent, named abilities that can be lifted out and used like ordinary routines. Knowing where multiplication occurs is not the same as knowing where “understands a supplier's exception” lives.
Yet the familiar request-and-response interface is often the first thing we build around it. That is useful. It can also conceal the part we have not learned how to separate.
Consider Docker and the software engineering practices around containers. They arrived through years of testing, adoption and adjustment. The AI application rush was trying to compress a comparable maturation into a couple of years. Two years versus decades. What could go wrong?
Plenty.
Zero or one: which part can another system call?
A modern AI application can look remarkably like an operating system, loosely speaking. Retrieval is part of its input/output path. Context resembles working memory. Agents resemble threads carrying out activities. These are analogies, not literal descriptions of an LLM's internals, but they help locate the work.
A model is invoked at a particular point in the agent flow. The orchestration framework supplies context, remembers intermediate results, chooses the next call and eventually returns an answer. Much of the application's useful behaviour lives in that arrangement around the model.
Now let a second system call it. Suppose the exposed choices are only:
Zero: call the base language model.
One: call the complete orchestrated application and receive its final answer.
Calling that final endpoint from an ordinary application may be entirely sufficient. But when one agent system needs to work with another, the choice is limiting. It may need the state reached halfway through a task, the evidence already collected, or a callback when a particular agent has finished. Starting again at the base model discards useful work. Calling the final endpoint asks for more work than the receiving system needs.
The problem is not that an API is incapable of carrying state. An application can persist memory and expose finer operations. The problem is that a wrapper which exposes only those two endpoints has not done so. Its caller cannot reach the internal memory merely because the application uses agents. And exposing that memory still says nothing about whether learned abilities inside the underlying model are independently reusable.
What we tried with YojnAI
With YojnAI, our approach was to wrap memory states in a data structure and keep caching those states so the application could expose callbacks at the agent level. A caller could work with an intermediate state instead of choosing only between the base model and the final orchestration endpoint.
This also let us “teach” the invoked LLMs to work with the wrapper's memory operations during the application flow. The wrapper kept the states; the model could use those operations. That is different from a neural network acquiring a memory subsystem we could lift out and transplant into another model.
We built utilities on top of that work and called them Apps. Different story. YojnAI's application design follows those parts through the work a customer needed to do.
But even that approach was not enough for the larger question.
A third possibility: combine the learned parts
What I really wanted was a third scenario: a subnet of one neural network working with a subnet of another. Not merely their final answers passing through an endpoint. The learned capacities themselves becoming composable.
Imagine a model M1 containing capacities I1, I2, I3, …, In, realised through subnets which might overlap. Another model, M2, contains capacities K1, K2, K3, …, Kn, again potentially overlapping.
How would you take K2 from M2, and I2 and I3 from M1, to make M3?
Note
Naming a capacity does not isolate it. The notation makes the question easy to write. It does not establish that those capacities are cleanly located, separable or compatible. Overlap is part of the difficulty. Removing the part we call I2 might also remove something I3 relies on. Two representations that work within their own models may not mean the same thing when connected.
There are two different times at which we might attempt the combination:
When the combination happens	The question it raises	
Before deployment, loosely like compilation	Can selected learned components be aligned and assembled into a new model which preserves the wanted capacities?	
During execution, loosely like runtime linking	Can one running system use a selected learned capacity in another, with the representations, state and dependencies needed for that interaction?	
Pre-deployment composition is a research problem of its own. Work such as Git Re-Basin examines a particular route to aligning and merging model weights. The runtime question reaches beyond what a request-and-response wrapper has solved. Transporting a message cannot, by itself, discover a decomposition of the learned computation or make incompatible representations fit.
That was the force of my complaint about the API model. The familiar interface can carry the eventual interaction. It cannot substitute for understanding what is being composed.
My gut said a blockchain might have a role here. A shared record could help parties coordinate contributions, versions or use. It would still need something meaningful to record. The road from a ledger to a working M3 is long and hard.
The inquiry continues in The intelligence between the parts. It asks what must pass between learned capacities for their combination to retain meaning. There is also nearer work we can do without claiming to have solved that problem: make the capabilities we already know how to share intelligible to their next user.
Several different things can look like intelligence
A model, a prompt, a dataset, a workflow and a hosted service can each contribute to a useful result, but the next team receives something different in each case. A dataset provides examples, a prompt supplies instructions in a context and a workflow connects operations. A model contains learned parameters, while an endpoint offers a response with much of its implementation remaining at the provider. These forms carry different dependencies and different opportunities to change the behaviour: adopting a prompt leaves the consumer to supply the model and its context, whereas invoking a service leaves more of the operation with the provider. A useful catalogue makes that contribution and continuing responsibility intelligible, so a team can discover the form it actually needs.

Each distinction changes what the checking step can do with the answer.

Object being supplied	A document-extraction workflow, not a trained subnetwork	
Input	A declared family of invoice documents	
Output	Supplier fields and payment terms, with source locations and unresolved values	
Required context	Document identity, language and the selected workflow version

body:
Reuse a capability
Another team has an invoice-extraction workflow you would like to use. It returns supplier fields and payment terms, with their locations in the document. Your application could use those results to prepare a payment for review. What must travel with the workflow for you to rely on it?
DAOnet connects discovery and reuse with execution, continuing memory and a shared account of the exchange. It is paused and remains a protocol design; this worked example explains the exchange rather than a running marketplace. Scope for any work on it is agreed through RawThoughts consulting.
Find out what the workflow returns
Suppose an invoice says “payment due 30 days after delivery” but gives no delivery date. The workflow should return the term and its location while leaving the due date unresolved. Your application can then ask for the delivery date. A guessed date would conceal the information the reviewer still needs.
Before adopting such a capability, the receiving team needs to understand which documents it supports, what it returns and what must be supplied by the application.
Important
Check both permissions. The workflow's licence governs reuse of the contribution. Permission to process the customer's invoices is a separate requirement.
Extraction supplies information for payment review; it does not approve or execute the payment.
Follow a version into the receiving application
Compare two hypothetical versions against the same invoice:
Version	Returned result	Consequence for payment review	
A	The payment term, its document location and an unresolved due date	The reviewer can inspect the term and request the delivery date.	
B	A proposed date without the supporting term or location	The reviewer cannot check where the date came from using this result.	
Version B could support more invoice layouts and still break this application's review. The team could keep A while its dependencies remain available, or return the invoice for manual handling. “Latest” does not tell a consumer whether a change is suitable.
To investigate a later problem, both teams need to identify the version used, the invoice and the returned output. That lets them distinguish an unsupported document from a changed result or an error in the receiving application. Versioning makes those dependencies visible as the capability travels beyond its first use.
Let use improve the next contribution
Reusing the workflow can also help improve it. In the design, a coordinating agent called CEO GPT arranges agents that use intelligences, the capabilities agents draw on, and playbooks from the marketplace. Their traces pass through DAOnet to ExpertGPT, the design’s name for the human-feedback service, which informs the next intelligences and playbooks offered for reuse.
In the invoice example, repeated confusion between a payment term and a delivery date could become a case for review. A reviewer could identify the distinction, help improve the extraction capability or its playbook, and make a revised version available to the next application. The version comparison still matters: receiving an improvement does not mean accepting it blindly.
The same traces connect use with credit for the contributors, although the calculation of credit and payment remains open. Recording a trace cannot itself improve a model or determine what somebody is owed; review and evaluation still have work to do.
After discovery: execution, memory and observability
Finding the workflow is only the start. Configuration connects it to your application; execution runs the chosen operation, such as extracting invoice terms. Memory keeps the invoice and its context connected across requests, so a later delivery date meets the right term.
Both teams also need to examine an attempt and its result. If the connection fails, did the request leave your application, did the workflow run, and did its answer return? Observability makes those events available to investigate.
DAOnet includes a ledger and smart-contract layer for shared transaction arrangements. Which arrangements need a chain, and which could use existing infrastructure, remains open.
What a shared record leaves to judgment
A shared record could identify the version used, the agreed use and the operation attempted. The payment reviewer still needs the extraction result and enough evidence to decide whether to approve it. Recording an approval also does not tell the participants whether a payment succeeded. They need an account of the result as well as the decision.
The choice of infrastructure follows that coordination problem. A common ledger could help participants compare their accounts of an exchange. It cannot supply a missing delivery date, judge an invoice or make an unsupported extraction reliable.
Reuse within one application and across applications
YojnAI approaches reuse within an application by arranging models, tools and checks for a particular operation. DAOnet's protocol extends reuse across applications and teams. Its practical question is whether sharing a capability saves the receiving team work while preserving what it needs to understand and review the result.

Your application can then ask for the delivery date. A guessed date would conceal the information the reviewer still needs.
Before adopting such a capability, the receiving team needs to understand which documents it supports, what it returns and what must be supplied by the application.
Important
Check both permissions. The workflow's licence governs reuse of the contribution. Permission to process the customer's invoices is a separate requirement.
Extraction supplies information for payment review; it does not approve or execute the payment.
Follow a version into the receiving application
Compare two hypothetical versions against the same invoice:
Version	Returned result	Consequence for payment review	
A	The payment term, its document location and an unresolved due date	The reviewer can inspect the term and request the delivery date.	
B	A proposed date without the supporting term or location	The reviewer cannot check where the date came from using this result.	
Version B could support more invoice layouts and still break this application's review. The team could keep A while its dependencies remain available, or return the invoice for manual handling. “Latest” does not tell a consumer whether a change is suitable.
To investigate a later problem, both teams need to identify the version used, the invoice and the returned output. That lets them distinguish an unsupported document from a changed result or an error in the receiving application. Versioning makes those dependencies visible as the capability travels beyond its first use.
Let use improve the next contribution
Reusing the workflow can also help improve it. In the design, a coordinating agent called CEO GPT arranges agents that use intelligences, the capabilities agents draw on, and playbooks from the marketplace. Their traces pass through DAOnet to ExpertGPT, the design’s name for the human-feedback service, which informs the next intelligences and playbooks offered for reuse.
In the invoice example, repeated confusion between a payment term and a delivery date could become a case for review. A reviewer could identify the distinction, help improve the extraction capability or its playbook, and make a revised version available to the next application. The version comparison still matters: receiving an improvement does not mean accepting it blindly.
The same traces connect use with credit for the contributors, although the calculation of credit and payment remains open. Recording a trace cannot itself improve a model or determine what somebody is owed; review and evaluation still have work to do.
After discovery: execution, memory and observability
Finding the workflow is only the start. Configuration connects it to your application; execution runs the chosen operation, such as extracting invoice terms. Memory keeps the invoice and its context connected across requests, so a later delivery date meets the right term.
Both teams also need to examine an attempt and its result. If the connection fails, did the request leave your application, did the workflow run, and did its answer return? Observability makes those events available to investigate.
DAOnet includes a ledger and smart-contract layer for shared transaction arrangements. Which arrangements need a chain, and which could use existing infrastructure, remains open.
What a shared record leaves to judgment
A shared record could identify the version used, the agreed use and the operation attempted. The payment reviewer still needs the extraction result and enough evidence to decide whether to approve it. Recording an approval also does not tell the participants whether a payment succeeded. They need an account of the result as well as the decision.
The choice of infrastructure follows that coordination problem. A common ledger could help participants compare their accounts of an exchange. It cannot supply a missing delivery date, judge an invoice or make an unsupported extraction reliable.
Reuse within one application and across applications
YojnAI approaches reuse within an application by arranging models, tools and checks for a particular operation. DAOnet's protocol extends reuse across applications and teams. Its practical question is whether sharing a capability saves the receiving team work while preserving what it needs to understand and review the result.

When you select text and choose a reading assistant, the link opens that provider with the selected passage, nearby context, the section and article titles, and the article and publication addresses. The provider's own terms, privacy policy and your account settings govern what it does with the request and any conversation that follows. Reading the article does not require using an assistant.

We keep no record of visits on our own systems; GitHub keeps its connection logs for the periods its policy sets. Correspondence you send is kept for as long as the matter it concerns needs it and as the law requires.
Security and incidents
This website holds no accounts and receives no form submissions. If a personal-data breach affects you, we inform you and the authorities as applicable law requires.
Your choices
Following another external link takes you to that service under its own data practices. Links to RawThoughts services lead to rawthoughts.in, which RTEPL publishes under its own privacy notice.

Requests are handled under applicable law; information needed to comply with a legal obligation or resolve a dispute may need to be kept. body:
Follow an incident
YOJN Care is not a live emergency or dispatch service; this guide explains its response design. If you need help now, call your local emergency number.
Imagine a shop camera detecting a person after closing time. A second camera supplies another view. An operator calls the owner to ask whether the person is authorised staff, but the shift ends before the owner replies. The next operator needs both views, the question already asked and the work still waiting. Starting again from the latest alert would lose part of the incident.
YOJN Care brings those observations and actions together, connecting the person asking for help with their community, monitoring operators and authorised responders.
Continue the incident, not just the latest alert
The operator compares the camera frames with the shop's reference view and instructions. A person in the image might be authorised staff; the pictures alone do not settle it. The operator records the call and the unanswered question. Later notifications add evidence to this incident instead of starting another investigation of the same event.
A neighbour may have opened the alert without agreeing to investigate. The incoming operator needs to know who has actually agreed to continue the review. Opening an alert, reviewing it and dispatching help therefore need separate states. The monitoring guide follows this handover, and Who carries the incident? explores the responsibility behind it.
Someone can ask for help directly
SOS begins with a person asking for help. It needs no camera image to make that request meaningful. High Alert raises a concern for assessment, as does an automatic detection; the reviewer needs to know which kind of request arrived.
Both personal actions are accessible with one hand. Groups, location sharing, camera sessions and incident evidence can give others context. After the gesture, the person needs to see whether the request is still sending, has reached the service or is being handled. Understand a personal request follows those states and what happens if the person corrects or cancels it.
Give the reviewer a usable view
Monitoring a shop starts with its existing cameras, the hours when nobody should be there and the owner's instructions. A computer at the premises, or compatible camera software, supplies detections and media for review. The installation, connection and cameras need continuing maintenance; an old image cannot answer whether somebody is still inside.
The operator also needs the earlier handling. An old image and an unanswered call leave different questions open: one needs a current view, the other an answer from the owner. The evidence path follows those inputs from the premises to the reviewer.
Keep someone available to continue
Sharing monitoring across premises and involving the community can make coverage more affordable. Grouping related observations also avoids asking several people to investigate the same thing from scratch. But somebody still needs to be available when a case arrives, and an unanswered case must remain visible while they work on it.
A response service needs agreed staffing, coverage, maintenance and authorised response arrangements. Emergency-service integration requires those services to participate; it cannot be supplied by a button in the application. Staffing and maintenance explains what continuing that coverage involves.

body:
Understand a personal request
YOJN Care is not a live emergency or dispatch service; this guide explains its personal interface. If you need help now, call your local emergency number.
You have pressed SOS. Did the request reach anyone, and has someone agreed to help? With one hand occupied and little attention to spare, you need to understand both. A moving indicator or a list of contacts cannot answer the second question.
SOS and High Alert start different reviews
SOS is a deliberate request for help unless activated accidentally. High Alert raises a concern for further assessment. The reviewer needs to know which arrived before deciding what to check; whether anyone has agreed to respond is a later question.
The emergency action stays visible. Distinct one-handed gestures for SOS and High Alert open a dedicated screen, where the person can follow the request. Groups, shared location and incident evidence help others understand the situation.
A request can begin without a camera view
A person asking for help should not need a camera image to make the request meaningful. A camera detection begins with an observation that needs interpretation. Care keeps these origins distinct, then follows what happens to each request:
State	What the person needs to know	
Sending	The application is trying to reach the service	
Received	The request reached the service, but someone may still need to pick it up	
Being handled	Someone agreed to review or respond; dispatch and arrival are separate events	
Correction requested	A change or withdrawal needs to reach anyone already handling the incident	
These distinctions matter even when a notification says “delivered” or “read”. A delivered message does not mean someone has taken it on. An opened message does not mean help is on the way.
When connectivity or setup blocks a request
If connectivity, a permission or incomplete setup prevents sending, the person needs to see that particular problem and reach the missing input or relevant phone setting. An urgent request should not send them through an unrelated administrative checklist.
The people view orders requests by urgency: unattended SOS, active SOS, unattended High Alert, then active High Alert. Family, friend and co-worker ordering applies within each group. A close relationship does not put a less urgent event ahead of someone still waiting for help. Nor does familiarity establish availability: who was notified and who agreed to act remain separate.
A correction needs to reach the continuing incident
Consider an accidental SOS. Cancelling before it is sent differs from correcting it after the service receives it. Someone may already be acting on the second request. Changing the local screen is not enough: the correction needs to reach those people, and the person cancelling needs to see whether it arrived.
Care's SOS flow carries the termination to the community separately from acknowledgement. The request's correction also needs to survive reconnection, so a delayed message cannot restore the earlier request without its update.
An interface with room to act examines these interaction choices. The monitor's view follows what happens when the request reaches another person.

body:
Review an incident and carry it onward
YOJN Care is not a live emergency or dispatch service; this guide explains its monitoring workflow. If you need help now, call your local emergency number.
You take over a shop incident from another operator. Two camera views are attached, the owner has been called and a reply is still awaited. Can you continue from there, or must you investigate everything again? Care brings the site's instructions, images, personal requests and earlier review together so the next person can see what happened and what remains to do.
Begin with the evidence actually available
A person appears in the shop during its unattended hours. The owner may recognise authorised staff; an operator may need a reference view or the owner's explanation before deciding what the image means. The detection begins that review.
Related frames and notifications belong together. One camera may show something another misses, and a later frame may change the interpretation. A judgment on one image should not close every observation in the incident.
A deliberate SOS has a different starting point: somebody asked for help. It can need attention even when no camera shows the situation. The reviewer needs to recognise that origin rather than see every alert as another camera-detection task.
Check whether the view can support the question
Suppose the shop camera appears connected, but its picture is old. It cannot tell you whether someone is still inside. You need a current view or an answer from the owner before drawing that conclusion.
Capture time and upload time therefore matter separately. So do unattended hours, camera placement, contact details and the site's instructions. Missing or unusable evidence needs to be apparent. The evidence path explains how keeping those inputs usable sustains the coverage.
Decide what the image means, then carry the answer onward
The review compares the frame with the reference view and the owner's instructions, distinguishing crime, suspicion, non-suspicion and a false positive. Selecting an answer and forwarding it are separate actions: the reviewer can reset an answer or leave it incomplete. Using the siren or speaker is separate too, with one person in control at a time.
A case cannot wait forever for somebody to pick it up. Care's automatic-detection workflow gives the operator a pickup allowance, then passes an unattended case to the manager and, after another timeout, to the community as suspicious. Loading evidence and calling the owner can extend handling time. The state and clock example sets out the allowances. They concern review, not the time for help to arrive.
Tell the next operator what still needs doing
In the shop incident, “owner called” is not enough. The handover needs to say that the reply is still awaited, which two views were examined and whether more camera notifications have arrived. The new operator can then continue without repeating the investigation or assuming the owner has answered.
The handover also needs someone who agrees to continue. A community contact may be unavailable, and an operator who can review images may have no authority to dispatch help. Opening an alert establishes neither commitment.
An authorised responder may act outside the interface. Without their update, the outcome remains uncertain. Closing a shift or moving the case to another queue should not turn that uncertainty into a completed response. Who carries the incident? develops this responsibility; Follow an incident connects the review to the personal application and the service arrangements it needs.

body:
Compose, inspect and improve an application
Your purchasing assistant has found the agreement and extracted its payment terms, but it is waiting for a delivery date. A reviewer could already check the terms while the customer supplies the date. Why should both wait for the assistant's final answer?
YojnAI lets teams participate in that unfinished work, connecting models, tools and checks with intermediate results people can inspect. This hypothetical purchase follows the application design from a source document to a reviewed change.
YojnAI is paused as a product. Delivery and integration remain available through RawThoughts consulting; this guide explains the application model.
Give each part of the purchase a job
An agent combines models and tools for one contribution, such as retrieving the agreement or extracting its payment terms. A playbook arranges agents and checks into a workflow: retrieve the agreement, extract the terms, check that each term has a source, then prepare the draft once the missing date arrives.
An application configuration connects that playbook to the customer's actual agreements, services and permitted access. A reviewer's knowledge can become a check where it is needed, rather than another instruction added to one large prompt. Configuring these apps, checks, tools, agents and models is the Create part of YojnAI.
A financial calculation needs the same care: named inputs, operations and conditional branches keep the chosen periods and definitions visible. The composition account follows those choices.
Continue without repeating completed work
An application that receives only a finished answer has little opportunity to contribute while the work is running. Agent-level callbacks and saved intermediate state give another person or component a place to inspect a result, supply missing context and continue.
In the purchase example, a reviewer could examine the extracted terms while the customer supplied the delivery date. Keeping the completed extraction would avoid running it again just to incorporate that date. The important distinction is between the work already available and the dependency still waiting for an answer.
Add a customer’s date and a reviewer’s correction without redoing work
The customer’s date and the reviewer’s correction should enter without discarding completed work:
Part of the request	After extraction	Customer supplies a date	Reviewer corrects a term	
Supplier and source	Available	Unchanged	Still useful if the same source applies	
Payment term	Available, awaiting review	Unchanged	Use the reviewed value	
Delivery date	Missing	Use the supplied date	Unchanged	
Purchase draft	Waiting for the date	Ready to assemble	Reconsider the part using the term	
Order placement	Not performed	Not performed	Not performed	
The date can unblock a draft without repeating extraction. A corrected term can change the draft without losing that date. An older response arriving after the correction must remain an earlier result; using it as the current term could undo the review. The composition account develops this example, including concurrent work.
Find the step that needs to change
Suppose the reviewer disputes the payment term. The final answer alone cannot say whether the assistant read the wrong agreement, used an old version or extracted the wrong value. An execution trace connects the run to its steps, inputs, outputs and metadata, giving the reviewer somewhere to look. Review a disputed answer follows this investigation.
Start the review with the application and version, then the trace and the particular step being judged. A feedback project keeps assessments together, so reviewers can compare a proposed change with its results. Access roles determine who can review; expertise weights determine how their judgments contribute to evaluation. Permission to submit feedback and knowledge of a financial calculation answer different questions.
This assessment and feedback work belongs to Improve. An administrator versions the feedback project and starts an improvement job. The team then inspects the result and chooses whether to use it. One-click reversion gives them a way back if the new version proves unsuitable.
Choose which version people use
Deploy connects an application configuration to customer requests through versions, runs and A/B tests. A correction can inform a candidate version while people continue using the current one. The team can evaluate the change before choosing it.

Compose, inspect and improve an application
Your purchasing assistant has found the agreement and extracted its payment terms, but it is waiting for a delivery date. A reviewer could already check the terms while the customer supplies the date. Why should both wait for the assistant's final answer?
YojnAI lets teams participate in that unfinished work, connecting models, tools and checks with intermediate results people can inspect. This hypothetical purchase follows the application design from a source document to a reviewed change.

A playbook arranges agents and checks into a workflow: retrieve the agreement, extract the terms, check that each term has a source, then prepare the draft once the missing date arrives.
An application configuration connects that playbook to the customer's actual agreements, services and permitted access. A reviewer's knowledge can become a check where it is needed, rather than another instruction added to one large prompt. Configuring these apps, checks, tools, agents and models is the Create part of YojnAI.
A financial calculation needs the same care: named inputs, operations and conditional branches keep the chosen periods and definitions visible. The composition account follows those choices.

Review a disputed answer
A reviewer says the supplier allows fourteen days, while the purchasing assistant returned thirty. Before changing the model, find the agreement and intermediate work behind that answer. The error may be in the source, the extraction or the choice of agreement version.
Note
Illustrative walkthrough. This purchase example explains YojnAI’s review and improvement design.
Find the agreement behind the disputed term
Start with the purchase, the application version and the agreement used for the disputed term. Check what the agreement said when the answer was produced, as well as whether it applied to this purchase.
What you find	What to investigate	
Another supplier's agreement was retrieved	Source selection	
The applicable agreement says fourteen days, but extraction returned thirty	The input and operation that produced the unsupported value	
An earlier agreement allowed thirty days	How the application chooses the applicable version	
An older result replaced a corrected term	The request and revision associated with that late result	
Suppose the earlier agreement allowed thirty days, but the purchase was governed by its fourteen-day replacement. Extraction read its input correctly. Correct the draft to use the applicable agreement and keep that version beside the term. The improvement needs to address source selection; teaching extraction to return fourteen in every case would introduce another error.
Keep useful work while reconsidering its dependents
The customer's delivery date can remain useful while the payment term changes. Reconsider the draft that uses the term, without asking for the date again or repeating unrelated work.
A late response still belongs to the request and source it answered. Keeping it in the history helps explain what happened. Treating it as current could undo the correction. The composition account follows those dependencies through the wider purchase workflow.
Choose the change that fixes the answer
A useful change might correct a source, replace a tool, add a check, clarify an instruction, revise the workflow or adapt a model. A YojnAI feedback project keeps that question with the evidence being reviewed. Permission to review and the expertise behind a judgment remain separate.
For this purchase, compare two source-selection changes. One always prefers the newest agreement. The other chooses the agreement effective for the purchase date and returns that version with the term. Both could return fourteen days today; only the second has a reason to return thirty for a purchase governed by the earlier agreement. If the date is missing, it should ask rather than silently choose the newest document.
Tip
Compare more than the reported failure. Try the proposed change against both purchases, an unresolved date and a late response. Check that it returns the applicable term, preserves the source and does not overwrite a correction. Also consider what it costs elsewhere: better selection that drops the evidence location makes review harder, and a stronger model may slow ordinary requests.
The review now has a specific proposal: choose by applicability, keep the agreement's identity and leave extraction alone when it reads the source correctly. Review the proposal and its results before choosing a version for the application. The application model places that choice within composition, deployment and feedback.
